Measured empirically with pi -p: a 20k-word prompt answers normally; 25k, 40k and 80k words return exit 0 with EMPTY stdout and EMPTY stderr — the same silent empty-turn failure a bad model id produces. So the real usable window is roughly 25-30k tokens, not 1.31M. In agent mode that surfaced as: request -> Cloudflare 400 (no body) -> pi reads it as 'Context overflow detected' -> auto-compacts at ~48-51k -> retries. All four workers compacted repeatedly at 48-51k while pi's status line said they were at 3.7% of 1.3M. wgi died outright: 'Context overflow recovery failed: Summarization failed: 408' — the recovery summarisation exceeded the same ceiling. Fix: modelOverrides now set contextWindow 24576 and maxTokens 8192 for both models, so pi compacts on its own schedule instead of discovering the limit through a provider rejection. Note this is separate from the 429 rate limit; the 400/408 family is this, the 429 is concurrency.

data.note:
2026-09-14 23:19 - ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND REPRODUCED. Supersedes both the description's claim and the previous correction note.

internal/runstate/store.go peek():

    s.git.run("fetch", s.remote, s.branch)
    head = s.git.run("rev-parse", "FETCH_HEAD")
    view = s.git.lsTree(head, Root)

FETCH_HEAD is ONE FILE in .git, shared by every process using that checkout. Any concurrent `git fetch` in the same repository overwrites it. The run then resolves FETCH_HEAD to whatever the OTHER fetch last wrote — typically main — and builds its view by ls-tree of that commit. main has no .ticfac tree, so the view comes back EMPTY.

The failure chain from there:
1. view empty -> Store.Checkpoint() reports exists=false
2. PutCheckpoint takes the CREATE path (CreateIfAbsent) instead of UpdateIfSHA
3. the push is refused (the branch ref moved)
4. peek() re-reads, finds checkpoint.json DOES exist on origin
5. put() returns ConflictExists
6. checkpoint() returns an error and the run exits

This is the only story that explains the exact outcome we captured. ConflictExists is reachable ONLY from the create path; a genuine concurrent checkpoint write by another reconciler would have produced ConflictStaleSHA.

REPRODUCTION (scratch repo, no ticfac needed):
  git fetch origin epic; git rev-parse FETCH_HEAD   -> epic head, view has .ticfac
  git fetch origin      ; git rev-parse FETCH_HEAD   -> main head, view is EMPTY
Confirmed 2026-09-14.

The trigger in both pwp deaths was my own watcher running `git -C <the run's checkout> fetch -q origin` every 15-25 seconds. But the defect is not the watcher. ANY concurrent fetch does this: an operator running git fetch, an editor's auto-fetch, a second tk command, a status script. ticfac tells operators to watch runs and then dies when they do.

SEVERITY IS HIGHER THAN A CRASH. s.head is also set from the clobbered FETCH_HEAD, so a writer can end up building a commit on the WRONG BASE. A crash is the good outcome; a write rooted at main's tree is the bad one. Check every use of s.head for that exposure.

FIX: never read FETCH_HEAD. Fetch into a private per-run ref and read that:
    git fetch --no-write-fetch-head origin +<branch>:refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>
    git rev-parse refs/ticfac/peek/<run-id>
A private ref is process-local state that no other git command touches. --no-write-fetch-head (git 2.29+) additionally stops ticfac from clobbering FETCH_HEAD for everyone else.

ACCEPTANCE: a test runs a plain `git fetch <remote>` against the run's checkout between two run-state writes and asserts the run continues and the epic completes; a second test asserts peek() resolves its head from the private ref and not from FETCH_HEAD.

2026-09-15 17:44 - HOW IT ENDED, and three further defects from the same incident.

The reconciler's own backstop fired (dispatch.go waitForSettlement: the wall clock plus one wipe threshold of grace) at 14:50:18 and refused the attempt RefusedUnaddressed, ending the run as failed. That bounded the stall at about 85 minutes instead of forever. The backstop is right. What it left is not:

1. THE REFUSAL'S REASON REACHED NO OPERATOR SURFACE. The feed goes straight from 'dispatched cwa' at 13:24:45 to a generic run_finished ('cwa did not pass: the run stopped rather than integrating over an unproven change…'). The checkpoint reason is the same generic text. The specific refusal — unaddressed, past the wall clock, release with ticfac settle — appeared nowhere a watcher reads. It had to be recovered by reading dispatch.go. A refusal that decides a run's fate must be a feed line with its own text.

2. THE REFUSAL'S WORDING IS FOR THE WRONG FAILURE. It says 'its supervisor never settled it, and a pid that outlives its job is a number the host reuses. Nobody can say whether it is running.' That text was written for the local subprocess executor's dead supervisor. Here herdr could say exactly: the agent was alive, working, and ignoring the interrupt. The refusal should name what the executor actually observed.

3. THE WORKER WAS ORPHANED. The run ended; the agent tick-cwa-a7 was still working and spending, in a workspace nothing will clean up. Refusing an attempt as unaddressed must not leave a live agent behind — the stop in this tick must run before the refusal, not after the run is gone.

Resuming the run does not recover by itself: the settlement deadline is derived from the durable dispatch marker, so a resumed run re-reads the same live agent past the same deadline and refuses again, and ticfac settle refuses to release an attempt the executor can still address. A person has to stop the agent first.

data.note:
2026-09-16 07:48 - FOURTH DEFECT FROM THIS INCIDENT, and it is the one that made the others unrecoverable.

reconcile/settle.go addressForSettlement built the settlement handle with Executor hardcoded to subprocess.ExecutorName. The herdr executor refuses a handle naming another executor — correctly — so releasing ANY herdr attempt failed:

  ticfac settle 9pd cwa 7: reconcile: inspect attempt 7 of cwa: handle names executor "local-subprocess"; this is herdr

That is the command the run's own refusal instructs the operator to run ('release it with ticfac settle … once you have looked'). So a herdr run that stopped needing a person offered the person a command that could not work. Every herdr run since the executor shipped has had this; nothing hit it before because no herdr attempt had needed a release.

FIXED BY HAND: the handle now carries marker.Executor, the executor the attempt was dispatched under, from its own durable marker. An older marker with no executor field leaves it empty, which both executors accept. Two tests: one that a marker's executor reaches the handle for herdr, subprocess and empty; and a guard that fails if addressForSettlement ever names one executor literally again — verified to fail against the committed version.

With it, attempt 7 of cwa released cleanly and the run can be resumed.

data.note:
2026-09-17 14:10 - Design decision, changed during implementation: on a refusal the run STOPS rather than draining the window.

Draining was the first instinct - the in-flight attempts are paid for, why abandon them? - but it is wrong. A failing gate leaves its tick's merge on the integration branch (that is what makes the documented repair 'fix the tree and run again'), so any attempt drained after it would gate against a tree already known to be bad and fail for a reason that has nothing to do with its own work. A run that manufactures failures for good work is worse than one that stops.

And nothing is lost by stopping: an in-flight attempt is durable - marker on the remote, commits on its own branch - and a resumed run adopts it by identity. That is not a hope; it is what happened to attempt 22 of 7zs this morning, dispatched by one incarnation and adopted, collected and closed by the next.

The acceptance item that said in-flight attempts are 'drained through their own gates rather than abandoned' is therefore replaced by: a refusal stops further dispatch, and every attempt still in flight is NAMED in the feed as still running and adoptable on resume.

At width 1 a tick's k-th try was reliably attempt k. At width N it is not: in the fixture a2 takes number 2, so a1's second try is attempt 3.

During epic-9pd's gates the system went low on memory twice, and each time the harness killed the operator's watcher as collateral - the run was never in trouble, but the thing watching it died. Two consequences worth designing for, not just the slowness already recorded here:
- A gate can kill things that are not the gate. Anything sharing the host - the watcher, another agent, the operator's editor - is a candidate victim.
- The failure is silent from the run's point of view. The run kept going and never knew its observer was gone, which is the stall shape this project keeps rediscovering: the orchestration was fine, the monitoring died.

Mitigation taken now: the watcher was rewritten leaner (no python per poll, 120s beat) and relaunched. That treats the symptom. 2026-09-18 13:23 - Epic retro written to .tick/logs/herd/9pd/RETRO.md (retros are gitignored by convention, as av8's and qeu's are). The verdict 9t5 asked for, recorded here because the tracker is what survives:

IS TICFAC READY TO RUN UNATTENDED? NO, and specifically.

It survived everything: 9 process deaths, a wedged docker daemon, a 2.5-hour ssh hang, a host driven to load 218, and five false gate refusals. Not one lost a worker's work - every attempt was adopted by identity on resume, every refusal named its repair, and when the operator tried to release a settled attempt the tool refused and said why. The durable-evidence doctrine held under conditions nobody designed for.

But it needed a person 11 times (run_held) plus a resume after each of 9 deaths. Most were not ticfac's fault - the orchestrator's monitoring, the host, a wedged daemon - and that is the problem: ticfac cannot yet tell a failure it should WAIT THROUGH from one it should STOP FOR. It stops for both, correctly, and a person decides. That is supervised, not unattended.

The blocker to name: 9da. An epic close-out on a repository declaring the PR + CI rule cannot complete itself, because the run's checkpoint writes move the PR head it gates CI on. Phase 3 is the first epic to run a close-out under that rule and it deadlocked; Phase 4 moves the reconciler to a host with no operator watching, where that is fatal rather than annoying.

Four defect classes, each found more than once, each now a tick: process-global git state (3 instances), external calls with no deadline (3), tests that sample a race rather than wait (5, tracked as cy2), and guards that cannot fail for the reason they were written (3, found by the review using mutation - the most valuable category, because those are the tests we were trusting).

Gate cost: 62 runs at ~20 minutes each at the start; now 3m26s, verified on two machines and in CI.

2026-09-18 16:11 - AMENDED (operator decision, 2026-09-18): the gate is no longer 'an epic completes unattended and merges its own PR'. It is 'an epic runs to completion unattended and stops at a PR that is REVIEWED and CI-VERIFIED, for a person to merge.'

Where the old wording came from: SPEC 12 Phase 4 says 'project w1z A1 again', and w1z's A1 reads 'An epic submitted with tk cloud run completes - waves, gates, merged PR - with the operator's laptop offline from submission onward.' The merge was never an independent decision; it fell out of 'laptop offline'. Nobody at a machine means nobody to merge.

Why it changed: the merge is the one step worth keeping a person in. Everything before it - the waves, the per-tick gates, the review, the close-out - is work a machine can prove it did. The merge is a judgement about whether to accept the work, and a PR that is reviewed and CI-verified is exactly the artefact a person needs to make it quickly.

So question 1 of this review changes: do not ask whether the run merged. Ask whether it reached a reviewed, CI-verified PR with no operator intervention, and COUNT the interventions. One is a failure. Merging is not one.

Two things this makes sharper rather than weaker:
- the review must actually be ON the PR. A verdict that exists only in the run's records is not a reviewed PR; the person merging has to read it where they merge.
- CI-verified means green on the head that would be merged, re-derived at close-out time. 9da's repair is what makes that honest when the run's own writes moved the head.

Note for whoever reconciles this upstream: SPEC 12 Phase 4 and ticks w1z A1 still say 'merged PR'. This repository's gate now disagrees deliberately. Amend the SPEC, or record there that ticfac's Phase 4 gate diverges and why.

I claimed the uncommitted work was 'one cleanup from gone' and 'recovered only because a person happened to look'. Both false. ticfac already takes a WIP snapshot at the wall-clock stop:

That is byte-for-byte the work I rescued by hand. The safety net exists and it WORKED. My rescue branch was redundant.

SO THE REAL DEFECT IS NARROWER AND DIFFERENT: the refusal never mentions the snapshot. An operator is told 'no-commits: the attempt branch carries no commit beyond the base' and given no hint that a commit holding an hour of work sits at a known ref. A safety net nobody is told about is barely a safety net — I had the mechanism's own output in front of me and still went and did it by hand.

- The no-commits refusal (and every wall-clock refusal) must NAME the WIP ref and its commit when a snapshot was taken, and say what it is: a snapshot, not evidence, never merged, here is how to look at it.
- A redispatch should be able to START from that snapshot rather than from the base, or the operator should be told plainly that it will not.
- Nothing needs building to PRESERVE the work. Delete that part of the original description.

The 'do not dispose a dirty worktree' item also needs re-examining: with a snapshot ref the worktree may be safe to remove, which makes kvn the whole of that problem.

Also recorded: the same mechanism ran for ef7 attempt 5 and its snapshot commit e66c5f03 is EMPTY. That is real evidence that ef7 produced nothing in sixty minutes, rather than an inference from a clean worktree.

So the dependency ran backwards. k4s comes first; xo2 becomes the retirement tick it describes itself as, after ncv proves the executor works.

data.note:
2026-09-19 17:59 - 2026-09-19 — measured evidence, from the API rather than inference.

Commit 12c1aa0 on epic/ncv carries FOUR check runs:

    contracts: completed/success
    go:        completed/success
    sandbox:   completed/success
    typescript:completed/cancelled

forge.go's CI() maps 'cancelled' through its default branch to CIPending — deliberately, and the comment argues the case well: cancelled 'is not green, and saying the report is green would be the false close this seam exists to prevent'.

The consequence nobody intended: that commit is pending FOREVER. A cancelled check run is never replaced unless something re-runs on that exact commit, and 'gh run rerun --failed' on a later workflow does not touch it. So a commit superseded mid-flight by the run's own checkpoint push is permanently unusable as an ancestor verdict — which is precisely what 9da's walk needs ancestors for.

So the three failure modes now compound:
  - cancel-in-progress kills CI the run's own pushes supersede (this tick)
  - a cancelled run reads as pending, forever, on that commit
  - 9da's walk needs a CONCLUSIVE ancestor, and these commits never become one

Confirmed healthy by contrast: 35f6e9f, re-run to completion, carries 4x completed/success and nothing else, and everything between it and the head touches only .ticfac/. That is the shape the walk is built for, so the walk itself is sound — it is being starved of conclusive ancestors rather than failing at its job.

Suggests the cheapest fix is even more clearly paths-ignore on .ticfac/**: a checkpoint that never starts a workflow also never cancels one, and never leaves a permanently-pending commit behind.

data.note:
2026-09-20 00:33 - 2026-09-19 — operator wants this now, for Phase 5's own throughput. Design agreed:

PART 1 (do first, small): the worker is FINISHED once its evidence is collected. Everything after — integrate, gate, close — is orchestrator bookkeeping, but finishTick disposes the worker LAST, so a worker slot is held for a worker that has already gone home. Dispose after collect and stop counting it against max_parallel; admit the next tick immediately. max_parallel bounds LIVE WORKERS (a model, a pane, CPU), not bookkeeping.

PART 2 (only if part 1 does not recover the wall clock): stop the finish blocking the loop, WITHOUT goroutines — internal/reconcile has zero by design and that is why a run is reconstructible. Make the finish a state machine the existing loop advances one step per round, as it already polls live attempts, which requires the gate to become start-and-poll rather than a blocking call. That would also give the gate its own bound and stall warning.

MUST NOT BREAK: finishing stays SERIAL (the gate judges the branch as it stands, and a refusal stops the run before anything else merges); excuseWindow keeps other live attempts polled and excused during a long finish; a newly admitted attempt still branches from the integration branch as it stands.

data.note:
2026-09-20 01:38 - 2026-09-19 23:37 — a second consequence, observed live and sharper than the throughput one.

While the run is inside finishTick it emits NOTHING: no feed events, and no liveness probes either, because both are driven from the same loop. Tonight epic dha sat 32 minutes with its last event 'integrated 6na' and no probe rows at all, while its gate ran normally under load. To anyone watching the feed the run was indistinguishable from dead — which is the exact failure dh1 was filed to end, reappearing one level up: dh1 taught the run to tell a wedged WORKER from a working one, and the RUN itself still cannot be told apart.

So the fix has a second acceptance: a run that is finishing a tick keeps saying so — the feed and the liveness probe continue while the gate runs. Even without part 2, part 1 should not leave the loop silent.

Related: w1j (the gate's duration depends on what else the host is doing; that 32 minutes was a 3m26s gate under contention from three workers and a concurrent full suite), k7p (watching a run from anywhere is worth nothing if the run goes silent for half an hour).
